extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecutors/patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether claim additional elements integrate a recited judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, product of nature) into a practical application under Step 2A Prong Two of the Alice/Mayo framework to determine patent-eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application; if it does, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B; if it does not, the claim is directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should evaluate whether the claim 'applies, relies on, or uses the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception' so the claim is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception. Use the considerations listed in the MPEP subsections to perform the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements in the functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element (or combination) may integrate the exception into a practical application if it demonstrates an improvement in the functioning of a computer or an improvement to another technology or technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the specification to determine if it discloses sufficient detail so that a person of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The claim must reflect components/steps that provide the improvement (though it need not literally state 'thereby increasing X'). This 'improvements' analysis at Step 2A does not consider whether the elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional. See cited cases (Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, Finjan, SRI Int'l) for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying or using the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that apply or use a recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition may integrate the exception into a practical application and thus not be directed to the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration is especially relevant to medical/diagnostic claims (Vanda example). Distinguish claims where administration steps are ancillary (data-gathering) versus claims that use the law of nature to inform therapeutic administration that reduces patient risk. Examples of treatment/prophylaxis include medication administration, surgery, dialysis, phototherapy, physiotherapy, organ transplants, acupuncture, radiation therapy, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementing the exception with a particular machine or manufacture integral to the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a particular machine or manufacture that is integral to the claim can integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the machine/manufacture is integral (not merely a generic computer) and whether claim limitations reflect specific machine-related features; see MPEP §2106.05(b) for detailed analysis and relevant case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting a particular transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that effects a transformation/reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing may integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed steps transform an article in a meaningful way (particular transformation test) as discussed in MPEP §2106.05(c) and relevant precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond mere linking to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the additional elements apply or use the judicial exception in a meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a technological environment or field of use, the claim as a whole may integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a catch-all consideration for meaningful limitations that impose more than a generic field-of-use limitation; see MPEP §2106.05(e) for examples and case analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merely reciting 'apply it' or implementing on a computer (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely reciting the words 'apply it' (or equivalent), including instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat generic statements to 'apply' an idea or routine use of a computer as meaningful limits. See MPEP §2106.05(f) and Alice/Benson precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception fails to integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for post-solution activity or steps that are merely nominal appendages to the exception; such insignificant limitations should not be considered meaningful limits (MPEP §2106.05(g); see Parker v. Flook example).

rubrics_metrics.name: General field-of-use/technological-environment linking (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere recitation of a technology field or environment, without meaningful limits, is insufficient (MPEP §2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of conventionality from Step 2A Prong Two
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A Prong Two specifically excludes consideration of whether the additional elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity; examiners must give weight to all additional elements regardless of conventionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even conventional or routine additional elements may integrate a judicial exception into a practical application under Prong Two; assess significance relative to the invention without discounting conventionality (contrast with Step 2B where conventionality is considered).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangibility/physicality is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element(s) is not a relevant consideration; physical implementation does not guarantee eligibility and non-physical elements do not doom eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on whether an element is physical/tangible; consider whether the element meaningfully limits the exception (see Alice, Genetic Technologies, Enfish, McRO examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of claim limitations matters (but is not standalone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specificity of claim limitations is relevant to evaluating considerations (e.g., particular machine, particular transformation, or whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception), but 'a specific way of achieving a result' is not by itself a stand-alone consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim provides specifics that reflect meaningful limitations and how those specifics affect the integration analysis. Lack of specific disclosure (e.g., Parker v. Flook) can indicate limitations are insignificant post-solution activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step evaluation procedure for Prong Two
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate integration into a practical application by (1) identifying any additional elements beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application using the listed considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all considerations will apply to every claim and the analysis is not a weighing test; evaluate the significance of additional elements relative to the invention, how limitations interact, and assess each claim on its own (dependent claims may be eligible even if an independent claim is not). See MPEP §§2106.04(d) and 2106.05 subsections for detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and claim coherence for demonstrating improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: To show an improvement to technology, the specification should provide sufficient detail so that one of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement, and the claim must reflect the components/steps that provide that improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conclusory assertion of improvement without substantive detail is insufficient. The claim need not explicitly state the improvement (e.g., 'thereby increasing bandwidth') but must include the elements that produce it. This supports finding integration under the improvements consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case-law examples to inform analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply and compare relevant Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Mayo, Alice, Enfish, McRO, Finjan, Vanda, Solutran, BASCOM, Roslin) to determine whether claimed additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples to identify whether limitations produced meaningful technological benefits (e.g., improved computer functionality, safer treatment regimens) or were mere field-of-use or post-solution activity. The MPEP provides detailed application of these cases for guidance.
